title: Campaign: caching across the estate
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 campaign-<tag> row, tag caching). Sources are 3 live campaign study quests from different repos per idea; recapAfter = any 3 sources passed. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: A cache key must include everything the cached answer depends on (user or tenant, resource, version); a shared cache keyed only on the URL serves one user's data to another.
ideas.why: Responses that depend on who is asking leak across users the moment a CDN or proxy caches them by URL alone.
ideas.prompt: A CDN starts caching GET /api/me/orders and customers see each other's orders. Explain the mistake and two ways to fix it.
ideas.answer: The URL is the same for every user, so the CDN serves the first user's orders to all of them. Mark personal responses private or no-store so shared caches skip them, or put the user in the key on purpose. For server-side caches, namespace keys with tenant, resource, id and a version.

ideas.idea: A write must invalidate (or update) every cached entry that shows the changed data, including lists and detail views, so readers do not see the old value.
ideas.why: Updating the detail entry but not the lists that contain the item leaves users seeing different values on different screens.
ideas.prompt: After editing an entry's title, the detail page shows the new title but every filtered list still shows the old one until reload. What should the update path invalidate?
ideas.answer: Every cache entry that renders the entry: its detail key and the list keys for every filter that could include it. Invalidating by a shared prefix (all list queries) or by tags attached to entries covers them in one call, instead of naming each filter combination.

ideas.idea: Decide which layer owns caching for each kind of data, and switch the others off for it, so two caches do not disagree about freshness.
ideas.why: A browser HTTP cache under a client query cache, or a page cache over a data cache, serves stale data that invalidating one layer does not clear.
ideas.prompt: A React app uses a query library with invalidation, yet after a save some screens show old data until a hard reload. The fetch wrapper uses default browser caching. What is happening?
ideas.answer: Two caches are in play: the query cache is invalidated, but its refetch is answered from the browser's HTTP cache. Let one layer own it: send API requests with cache: 'no-store' and let the query cache decide freshness, or the reverse. Clear layers from the inside out when several must stay.

ideas.idea: When a popular key is missing, let one caller load it while the others wait for that result, so a miss costs the origin one load, not hundreds.
ideas.why: A popular key expiring under load sends every concurrent request to the database at once: a stampede that can take it down.
ideas.prompt: A hundred requests miss the same product key at the same instant. Today the database runs the query a hundred times. What do you change, and what else lowers the risk?
ideas.answer: Coalesce the misses: the first request starts the load and stores the promise under the key, the others await that same promise, so the origin runs once. Add jitter to expiry times so related keys do not all expire together, and consider serving the stale value while one refresh runs.

ideas.idea: The database stays the source of truth; a cache holds only data you can lose and rebuild, never state such as idempotency records or balances.
ideas.why: Keeping authoritative state only in a cache loses it on eviction or restart, and the system silently forgets what it promised.
ideas.prompt: A team proposes keeping idempotency records and village resource counts only in Redis because it is fast. What do you say, and what may Redis hold?
ideas.answer: Records whose loss would cause duplicates or wrong balances belong in the database, written transactionally. Redis may hold copies you can rebuild from the database (cached reads, rate-limit counters, presence), so an eviction or restart only costs speed, never correctness.
